full_judgment:
Sheikh Hassan Arif, J: Since the questions of law and facts involved in the aforesaid writ petitions are almost same, they have been taken up together for hearing, and are now being disposed of by this common judgment.

 

2. The petitioners in the aforesaid writ petitions are either plaintiffs or defendants in Land Survey Tribunal cases filed by them or their opponents before the Land Survey Tribunals concerned as established by the Government throughout the country under section 145A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (hereinafter called "the said Act") in order to determine the correctness of record-of-rights finally published through revision of the same under section 144 of the said Act. Being aggrieved either by orders passed by such Tribunals or judgments and decrees passed by them, the petitioners approached this Court and obtained the instant Rules calling in question the said orders, judgment and decrees.

 

3. One of the main grounds taken by the petitioners in approaching this Court under writ jurisdiction is that the Government has not yet established any Land Survey Appellate Tribunals under section 145B of the said Act so that they can get legal redress by filing appeals against the said orders, judgments and decrees passed by the concerned Tribunals.

 

4. The orders, judgments and decrees, which are called in question in the instant writ petitions, are narrated in the table below for ready reference:—

5. The petitioners in the above mentioned writ petitions have taken various grounds on merit assailing the impugned orders, judgments and decrees concerned. Some of them even referred to various evidences which have been considered, or allegedly not considered, by the concerned Tribunals.

 

6. In the course of hearing, learned advocates appearing for the parties have referred to a judgment (not yet released) delivered by a Division Bench of this Court comprising his Lordships Mr Justice Moyeenul Islam Chowdhury and Mr Justice Md Ashraful Kamal in Suo Motu Rule No. 3 of 2015. According to them, the said Suo Motu Rule, as issued by the said bench seeking a mandamus on the government to establish Land Survey Appellate Tribunals, has been made absolute vide judgment and order dated 25-7-2019 with a direction upon the government to establish such Appellate Tribunals within a period of 90(ninety) days from receipt of the copy of the said judgment.

 

7. Learned advocates in the instant writ petitions have argued, at length, various issues regarding the evidences on record and tried to make reference to different evidences from the lower Court records of the cases concerned, as have already been sent to this Court. However, this Court is of the view that disposing of such issues by this Court under writ jurisdiction will encompass re-examination and re-assessment of evidences, as adduced by the parties before the Tribunals, which is not permitted under writ jurisdiction.

 

8. As against this aspect, we have examined the relevant provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, in particular Chapter-XVIIA of the same as inserted vide section 2 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 2004 (Act No. 09 of 2004). For the purpose of the revision of the record-of-rights in respect of the Lands in Bangladesh, as provided by section 144 of the said Act, the government has in the meantime promulgated Tenancy Rules, 1955 specifying the stages of works to be conducted by the concerned Revenue officials and Land Field Officers. In such exercise of different functions at different stages, when a draft record of right is published under Rule 29 of the said Tenancy Rules by the concerned Revenue Officer, the aggrieved person has the right to file objection against the same under Rule 30 of the said Rules. After disposal of such objection upon hearing the parties, the aggrieved person will have the right to prefer appeal under Rule 31 of the said Rules to the Revenue Officer appointed with the additional designation of Settlement Officer or additional designation of Assistant Settlement Officer. Once such appeals are disposed of, the final record-of-rights in respect of the concerned land are prepared, if such orders of the Appellate Authority are not interfered with in the meantime on some limited grounds including fraud under Rules 42 and 42A of the said Rules. The matter does not end there, even after final publication of record-of-rights, the aggrieved party has been given an opportunity to challenge any entry in the said final record-of-rights by filing a suit before the Land Survey Tribunals concerned as established by the government in exercise of its power under section 145A of the said Act specifying the territorial limits and jurisdiction of such Tribunals. Such Tribunals have been empowered by the said provision only to entertain suits challenging the entry in the finally published record-of-rights as stated above. Such Tribunals have also been empowered by the said provision to declare the concerned record-of-rights to be incorrect and further to direct the concerned office to correct such record-of-rights in accordance with its decision and may also pass such other orders as may be necessary.

 

9. Obviously, because of such scheme as provided by the parliament through the aforesaid insertion of the Chapter XVIIA in the said Act and the Rules made there-under, thousands of citizens and persons approached such Tribunals with numerous suits challenging the entries in the finally published record-of-rights. Consequently, such Tribunals comprising of Joint District Judges have been flooded with various number of cases. Since the Tribunals have been given the powers to dispose of such cases in accordance with the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, so far as the same is not inconsistent with the provisions of the said Act, in respect of certain matters mentioned tinder section 145B of the said Act, thereby making the Tribunal a quasi-civil court having limited powers of the Civil Court, the same have disposed of, or are in the process of disposing of, the said numerous number of suits. In such process, the litigants before the Tribunals have every reason to become aggrieved either against any order passed by the Tribunals in interlocutory matters or against judgment and decrees passed by them after conclusion of hearing. In such circumstances, it appears, the said huge number of litigant persons found themselves in a very helpless position to challenge or assail such orders, judgments and decrees passed by the said Tribunals in view of the admitted position that the government has not yet established any Land Survey Appellate Tribunal for giving redresses to the said aggrieved litigants in appeals to be filed by them against the said orders, judgment and decrees.

 

10. It may be mentioned here that in accordance with the provisions under sub-section (4) of section 145B of the said Act, judgments, decrees or orders passed by the said Land Survey Tribunals are appealable and, as such, it was necessary and incumbent on the part of the government to establish such required number of Land Survey Appellate Tribunals in exercise of its power under section 145B immediately after the establishment of the Land Survey Tribunals concerned. Given that even the orders passed by the Land Tribunal Tribunals are appealable orders, the government was not in a position to wait for any further time to establish such Appellate Tribunals in view of the probability that even on the very day of filing of a suit before the Tribunal, a litigant may become aggrieved by any order passed by the Tribunal.

 

11. In the Course of hearing, Md Dider Alam (Kollol), learned advocate in Writ petition No. 5434 of 2017, has drawn this Court's attention to a gazette notification published by the government on 5-11-2012. The said gazette is quoted below:— "এস আর ও নং ৩৭১-আইন/২০১২।—State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (Act No. XXVII of 1951) এর section 145B এর sub-section (1) এবং (2) এ প্রদত্ত ক্ষমতাবলে সরকার এতদ্বারা ল্যান্ড সার্ভে আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনাল, ঢাকা প্রতিষ্ঠা করিল এবং ইহার স্থানীয় অধিক্ষেত্র হইবে সমগ্র বাংলাদেশ”।

 

12. It appears from the above quoted gazette that by this gazette, the government has established. Land Survey Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka giving it entire territorial jurisdiction of Bangladesh. There is nothing in that gazette as to who would be the judges of the said Appellate Tribunal or as to where the said Tribunal shall have its seat. Learned Deputy Attorney-General, present in Court, also has not given us any information as regards any other further steps as taken by the government pursuant the said gazette.

 

13. Nevertheless, even after publication of the said gazette, this Court issued the said Suo Motu Rule on 3-3-2015, being Suo Muto Rule No. 3 of 2015, and, according to the information given by the learned advocate concerned, the said Rule has been made absolute on 25-7-2019 with the direction upon the government to establish as many Land Survey Appellate Tribunals as may be required to hear appeals arising out of judgments, decrees or orders of the Land Survey Tribunals in Bangladesh. There is nothing on record as well as in the submissions of the learned Deputy Attorney-General that the government has taken any steps as of today for establishing such Appellate Tribunals which may function properly. Therefore, huge number of litigants, who are aggrieved by different orders, judgments and decrees passed by the Land Survey Tribunals, are now moving from one bench to another bench of the High Court Division with writ petitions to get redress. However, as stated above, in order to give such redress, we are required to reassess or reexamine the evidences adduced by the parties before the Tribunals concerned, which is not possible under writ jurisdiction. Though the statute, in particular section 145B of the said Act, provides that the government 'may' establish Land Survey Appellate Tribunals to hear the appeals arising out of the judgment and decree or order of the Land Survey Tribunals, with the establishment of Land Survey Tribunals in the meantime, this Court is of the view that, this 'may' as used in the said provision must be read as 'shall'. Otherwise, the entire purpose of the provisions under Chapter XVIIA of the said Act will become useless.

 

14. In view of above, we have no option but to express our frustration because of the failure of the government in establishing required number of Land Survey Appellate Tribunals and appointing judges therein. This being so, we find partial merit in the Rules, in so far as seeking direction on the government for establishment of such Tribunals is concerned, and, accordingly, said part of the Rules should be made absolute.

 

15. In the result, the Rules are made absolute in part. The respondent-government, in particular the concerned Ministries, are directed to establish as many number of Appellate Tribunals, appoint judges in those Tribunals and determine the seats of such Tribunals through such appointment by publishing gazette under section 145B of the said Act within a period of 90(ninety) days from receipt of the copy of this judgment. At the same time, since we are not in a position to determine the merit of the cases before us, which may only be determined by the Appellate Tribunals to be established by the government, the parties will be at liberty to address those issues before the Appellate Tribunals to be constituted by the government by preferring appeals before it. Thus, till the establishment of such Land Survey Appellate Tribunals and filing of such appeals by the litigants concerned, the parties should maintain status-quo in respect of the position and possession of the lands in question. Accordingly, operation of the impugned judgments, decrees and orders shall remain stayed till such filing of appeals. Parties are directed to maintain status-quo in respect of the position and possession of the land in question till filing of such Appeals by them before the Land Survey Appellate Tribunals to be established by the government. In preferring such appeals, delay occurred in the meantime shall be condoned.

 

16. Let the Lower Courts' Records, which have already been sent and tagged with the concerned writ petitions, be sent down to the concerned Tribunals.

 

Communicate this.

 

End.
